en: "By way of being easy to understand" means that since what is easy to understand can be inferred by oneself, it is precisely the difficult subject that first gives rise to the desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*) among the wise; such is the sense. And thus, by way of the connection of occasion (*avasara-saṅgati*), following experience—
The meaning is "the examination of recollection. For in that case—namely, regarding recollection—it would not be recollection;

the meaning is that this is because the experience has perished. Now, one might object: the causality of the experience is through its operation (*vyāpāra*), and that consists in being either the experience itself or its own operation existing at the moment immediately preceding the effect.
And since that [memory] remains unimpaired because the impression produced by it persists even when the experience has perished, he says:
"having a cause of a similar kind. [He adds: "because it has perished.
The sense is that even such causality is not possible in the case of the experience itself. By that very same [factor] which destroys the impression...
The meaning is that [the impression] acts solely through a memory of the same type, by means of another intermediate impression;
for it is impossible for the memory to be a cause in its own form, since it perishes in the third moment.
This refers to the result, which consists of successive memories directed toward each individual object.
"Because it lacks the capacity to destroy the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). The sense is that it lacks the same cognitive form (*samānaprakārakatva*).

"Of time or of disease": the sense is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the aforementioned collective mental representation (*samūhālambana*) would never be destroyed.
This does not entail an undesirable consequence, because there is a necessary rule that whatever is a produced entity (janyabhāva) is perishable. Now, one might object:

if time (*kāla*) and so forth were the causes of destruction by virtue of their being "time-ness" (*kālatva*) and so on, then it would follow that every mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is momentary; whereas if they were such causes by virtue of being specific individuals (*tadvyaktitva*), there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*). To this, he says: "of the final fruit."

The meaning is that one must postulate a distinct species (*vaijātya*) in the final fruit and state that it possesses the capacity for destruction by virtue of that specific form. "Not successive" means that there is no recollection following another recollection.
Because it is the referent of the term "firmness," one does not recollect again and again.

The meaning is this: the production of a more firmly established latent impression (*saṃskāra*) occurs, however, through the repeated recollection of an existing impression itself; thereby, the simultaneous presence of the factors that trigger awakening arises instantly, and from that awakened [impression], further recollection follows. Regarding the phrase "doubt concerning deviation" (*vyabhicārasaṃśaya*):

The meaning is that if "being an experience" (*anubhavatva*) were the reason, there would be a doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Thus, the point is that there is no lack of knowledge of deviation with respect to a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*). [This is stated] because of the absence of doubt regarding deviation;
for in a case where [the object] has been experienced only once, the final recollection—which destroys the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—is absent at that time.

The point is that because there is no absence of the destruction of the latent impressions (saṃskāra), even if [the cognition] is a cause by virtue of being an experience, there is no doubt regarding a deviation (vyabhicāra). Although the complexity (gaurava) of postulating infinite latent impressions and their destructions is not a defect because it is "aimed at the result" (phalamukha), otherwise...

For, out of fear of the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), there would be the undesirable consequence of dissolving the causality [of memory] toward inference by way of its being a qualified cognition; nevertheless, if causality is established by way of being a cognition (*jñānatva*),

then the distinction of that specific instance of memory which is of the nature of indifference (*upekṣā*) must be included within the scope of the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) of the cause.

In this context, since respect (*gaurava*) functions as a cause for memory by virtue of its being experienced, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in not introducing the distinction between various individual instances of memory; thus,
because the presence of the catalyst consisting in the knowledge of parsimony renders the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra-śaṅkā*) ineffective.
This is the purport. Thus ends the examination of recollection (smaraṇa). [Regarding the phrase] "because it is a produced direct perception" (*janyasākṣātkāratvāt*):
the term "produced" (*janya*) is included to exclude the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of God’s direct perception.

Now, one might object: "On account of extreme parsimony (*lāghava*), let the skin-sense organ (*tvagindriya*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*) be the instrument"; therefore, he says: "In this way" (*evam*).

"By virtue of being the substratum of the non-inherent cause's conjunction. The meaning is that there is a rule that every positive effect must have a non-inherent cause. "And if that [mind] were all-pervading": the sense is that its non-proximity would not be possible if the mind were all-pervading. Likewise...

"Satīti" means that even when the collection of visible causes is present, one must admit a delay in the effect due to the delay caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa). "Cakṣurādīnām api" means that the occurrence of visual perception and its absence can be accounted for by the presence or absence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), such is the sense.

"Because of being erroneous" means that the fault lies in the occurrence [of cognition] at an immediately preceding time; this is the sense. "The justification for both" means that when the mind is contracted, there is a connection with only a single sense organ, and thus only one cognition arises, whereas in the case of expansion...
The point is that the simultaneous occurrence of multiple cognitions through various sense organs is possible due to the mind's connection with them.
Although at the time when the mind is in contact with various sense organs— and specifically at the time when visual cognition (*cākṣuṣa*) and so forth arise—
there is no arising of gustatory cognition (*rāsana*) and so forth, [this is because] the visual causal complex (*sāmagrī*) acts as an obstacle to the gustatory and other cognitions.

The intention is that since the explanation is established by [the mind's] being an obstructer alone, there is no sublation even if the mind were all-pervading; nevertheless, there is complexity (gaurava) in such an obstructing nature. Nor does it follow that because the contact between the skin and the mind is the cause of cognition in general, the tactile causal complex must necessarily exist at the time of the visual causal complex.
It should not be said that the perception by touch (*spārśana-pratyakṣa*) of an atom is unavoidable even under the view that the mind is atomic;

for, as a last resort, one must accept that the causal complex of visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-sāmagrī*) and so forth acts as an inhibitor with respect to tactile perception. Even so, [the same would apply] to gustatory perception (*rāsana*) and other types of direct perception.

This is because the parsimony resulting from not having to postulate that [skin-contact] is an obstacle to the causal complex for visual perception and so forth is unimpeded in the case of the atomicity [of the mind]. Alternatively, the intention is that skin-mind contact is not a cause for cognition in general. For this very reason...
As was stated previously, cognition is not produced by other [senses] such as the skin because of their lack of connection;

and it has already been demonstrated that just as the contact between the skin and the mind, while being a non-producer of cognition in general, nevertheless accounts for the absence of cognition during deep sleep, so too [is it explained] in the case of the all-pervasiveness of the mind. Thus, regarding the all-pervasiveness of the mind...

The conjunction between the self and the mind is untenable because, in the view that [all things] are all-pervading (vibhu), there is no action in either the self or the mind; consequently, a conjunction produced by action is impossible, and there is no evidence for an unproduced conjunction. Furthermore, as for the claim that the minds are merely material atoms, this is untenable given that [the self] possesses infinite attributes and is distinct [from them].

The claim made by the Neo-logicians— that since it is logical for only those substrata (*dharmin*) already established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) to function as causes in their specific form, the restriction [of causality] arises from the influence of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)— is also not correct;
for that [cause] whose absence results in the non-production of an effect during deep sleep is precisely what is required.

For the mind must necessarily be admitted [as the substratum]. Nor should it be argued that the non-production of effects during deep sleep is due solely to the obstruction by a specific time; for there would be the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava) in assuming an infinite number of specific times as obstructing factors.

Nor does the objection that the same problem persists because the conjunction with a neutral mind exists even at the time prior to deep sleep apply; for it must be stated that the mind itself, drawn by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*),
is the cause of cognition and so forth, and in comparison to that, it is only the material atoms drawn by that specific unseen force [that are the cause].

It should not be said that its being the cause of that [smell] is appropriate; for if it were material, there would be no decisive factor (vinigamaka) as to whether it is earthness or water-ness and so forth, and if both were postulated, there would be a confusion of universals (jātisaṅkara). Having this in mind, it was stated: "In brief. Thus.

The explanation of the category of substance (dravyapadārtha). || 85 || Intending to establish the connection by way of the occasion (avasara-saṅgati), he says: "having defined substance. The sense is that once that [substance] has been defined, the obstructing desire to know [it] ceases.
This is the reading: "iti ced idam. Now, [one might ask] regarding the universal of color-ness (rūpatva) or existence (sattā):

Anticipating the objection that there might be a delimiting factor (avacchedakatva) for the causality residing in the quality [of color], he says: "Not so. By the phrase "color-ness, etc.," taste-ness and so forth are included. Although perception itself is the proof for the genus "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) in respect to color and the rest, by means of the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherently-connected (*saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*).

Although the perception of "quality-ness" (guṇatva) is possible [in visible qualities], nevertheless, because such perception is impossible in the case of supersensible color and so forth, the coexistence of "quality-ness" with those [supersensible instances] is not tenable; thus, inference has been demonstrated. Nor is there an establishment of "quality-ness" in supersensible color and so forth out of fear of its commingling (sāṅkarya) with "color-ness" (rūpatva) and other such categories.

It should not be argued that the demonstration of inference is useless because the existence of [gravity] and so forth is established by the very means of cognition that apprehends its substratum (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). For even in the case of color and other qualities, perception as "a quality common to all, including the ignorant" is not established. This is what must be understood here: there is one [universal] common to all qualities.
Since causality does not exist at all, how can the universal *guṇatva* (the quality-ness) be established as its delimiting property (*avacchedaka*)?

Nor should it be argued that the universal *guṇatva* is established as the delimiting property of all such causalities collectively— where each individual causality residing in the twenty-four qualities constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*).
If that were the case, then by the inference— "The causality residing in that which possesses a generality distinct from the form of substance-action must be delimited by some property"—
there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of establishing even a specific universal (vaijātya) common to the twenty categories, which is distinct from the form of color (rūpa).

Since spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is never a cause [of anything], and since the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is over-extended [to other categories], it cannot serve as a defining characteristic (*anavacchedaka*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "because of over-extension to action and so forth" (*karmādāvativyāpteḥ*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes generality (*sāmānya*).
He demonstrates the presence of the definition within the definiendum with the words "for it exists" (*bhavati hi*).
He states the purpose of the phrase "delimitor of the pervasion of substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpakatāvacchedaka*) as follows: "substanceness" (*dravyatvam*).
He states the function of the word "genus" (*jāti*) as follows: "the state of being substanceness" (*dravyatvatvam*).

To prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to substances and so forth by taking the genus in the form of "existence" (*sattā*), he adds "distinct from existence" (*sattābhinnā*). Even so, [there remains the problem] regarding the state of possessing generality (*sāmānyavattva*).
Regarding the word "existent" (*satī*): he states the purpose of the two qualifiers and the qualified [term] with the words "of genus, etc.
(*jātyādīnām*). "Therein" means among those [categories]. "Because of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to space, etc."—by "etc.," time and so forth are included.
This is according to the literal reading; [the definition is]: "being possessed of generality (*sāmānyavattva*), and being other than action (*karmānyatva*)."
There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because [the definition] possesses a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) that distinguishes the categories of action (*karma*) and so forth.

The reading "by means of velocity (*vega*), the restorative force (*sthitisthāpaka*) is also to be indicated" is intended to show that the word "velocity" refers to any latent impression (*saṃskāra*) other than mental disposition (*bhāvanā*). This is merely an illustration.
In the phrase "and velocities" (*vegāśca*), by means of the particle *ca* which serves to aggregate what has not been mentioned, gravity (*gurutva*) is also included.

Now, one might object that "being a quality of the corporeal" (*mūrtaguṇatva*) means "being a quality residing in the corporeal," and this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) because it applies to number (*saṃkhyā*) and other such qualities; therefore, he says:
"in non-corporeal [substances]" (*amūrteṣu*). Thus, the intended definition of the qualities shown is "being a quality that does not reside in non-corporeal [substances]."
The meaning is "homogeneity" (*sādharmya*). Nor should it be argued that this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) with respect to number (*saṃkhyā*), which resides only in corporeal things;

for [the definition refers to] being a quality (*guṇatva*) devoid of any genus (*jāti*) subordinate to quality-ness (*guṇatva*) that resides in qualities belonging to incorporeal things and is distinct from the universal of formative impression (*saṃskāratva*).

Alternatively, what is intended [by the definition] is the possession of a genus residing in quality that is delimited by being pervaded by corporeality (*mūrtatva*). Here, in the first case, numbers and so forth, as well as cognition and so forth, are excluded by the phrase ending with "void" (*śūnya*);
and the phrase "other than the nature of momentum" (*saṃskāratvānyā*) is included to encompass velocity (*vega*) and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).

By the second [qualification], namely "limited by another," number-ness (*saṃkhyātva*) and the like are excluded; by the [qualification] ending in "residing in [the substance]," object-ness (*karmatā*) and the like are excluded. In the root text, at the phrase "these are the formless qualities" (*ete 'mūrtaguṇāḥ*), one should understand that there is an elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., it should be read as *ete na mūrtaguṇāḥ*). Now, by the root text beginning with "dharma" (*dharmetyādi*), the status of these [qualities] as qualities residing in formless [substances] is established.
The previously stated common property (sādharmya) is over-extensive (ativyāpta) with respect to number and so forth; therefore, he says: "among corporeal [substances]" (mūrteṣu).

The meaning is that their common property is simply the quality of residing in corporeal substances. Nor should it be argued that even so, there is still over-extension with respect to number and so forth, which reside only in incorporeal [substances].

[The definition is] either: the state of being a quality that is devoid of any genus subordinate to quality-ness which is coextensive with [the qualities of] corporeal substance, quality, function, and latent impression;

or the state of possessing a genus that does not reside in dimension and which is the delimitor of the pervasion of the absence of corporeality; or the state of possessing a genus that does not reside in dimension and which is the delimitor of the pervasion of the absence of corporeality.

Because it is intended to be so stated: in the first [definition], by the phrase "ending with 'void' (śūnya)," numbers and so forth, as well as color-form and the like, are excluded. The term "pervaded by the universal *guṇatva*" (guṇatvavyāpya) is included to prevent the impossibility [of the definition] in the case of existing things that are not qualities. The inclusion of the *guṇatva* which serves as the substantive is to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to action (*karman*). In the second [definition], the inclusion [of the qualifier] is to prevent over-extension by taking the universal "supreme largeness-ness" (*paramamahattvatva*).

Regarding the phrase "residing in both" (*parimāṇāvṛttīti*): Now, by the root text stating "the qualities of both," it was asserted that the common property (*sādharmya*) of the five [qualities] beginning with number is their residing in both; however, since that would over-extend (*ativyāpta*) to [other qualities] such as color (*rūpa*), he explains the word "both" as referring to the corporeal (*mūrta*) and the incorporeal (*amūrta*)—namely, "corporeal and incorporeal. Nor...
It should not be said that [the definition] is over-narrow (*avyāpta*) with respect to number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth, which reside only in corporeal things (*mūrta*).

This is because what is intended is either "possessing a genus (*jāti*) subordinate to *guṇatva* (quality-ness) that resides in what resides in time," or "possessing a genus that delimits the co-extensive pervasion (*samavyāpaka*) of *dravyatva* (substance-ness). Now, as for "residing in more than one" (*anekāśritatva*):

Since the term "aneka" (many) lacks application in cases such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because it denotes a plurality qualified by multiplicity, he says: "conjunction," etc. Thus, the term "aneka" signifies that which is qualified by a number other than unity; therefore, there is no lack of application (*avyāpti*) in those instances.

Some maintain that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case, because what is intended is the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) which coexists with the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) whose counter-correlate is its own substratum. [This concludes verse] 89. Regarding the root text’s phrase "subsisting in each one," it refers to that oneness (*ekatva*) which is not delimited by the counter-correlate-ness of a mutual absence coexisting with itself.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is:

"those which are the counter-correlates (pratiyogin) of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) that pervades the mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) residing in their own substratum. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), because the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed after words such as *vinaya* in the sense of the base itself; thus, it applies to the word *viśeṣa*.

The sense is that because [the term] *vinaya* and so forth are included therein, they belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended categories). "The meaning is 'particular qualities' (*viśeṣaguṇa*)" means that the state of being a particular quality consists in being other than those things which, while not being *bhāvanā*, are inherent in what is excluded from the touch residing in air— that is, being other than those [qualities] which do not reside in air.

The definition is: being a quality other than heaviness and adventitious fluidity. Here, the term "quality" (guṇatva) is included as a qualifier to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to universals (*jāti*) and so forth.
The phrase "heaviness and so forth" is included to exclude heaviness and adventitious fluidity themselves. The word "other" (*anya*) is included to include natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*).
The term "existent" (sat) is included to exclude conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other such relations.

The first part ending in "other than" (*anya-anta*) serves as a qualifier for the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) within the definition of "existent" to avoid the under-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition to mental impressions (*bhāvanā*). The inclusion of "being" (*sat-tva*) and so forth is intended to prevent the impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) [of the definition] by taking into account [the existence of] being and the like.

And [the phrase] "contact and concealment" is for the purpose of including contact. To prevent the misconception that— by the etymological analysis of "that which has number as its beginning" and "that which has posteriority at its end"— only dimension and posteriority are being grasped, the qualities included by the word "etcetera" (ādi) are specified:

He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "number, dimension," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "gravity and velocity" in the root text (*mūla*), the term "velocity" (*vega*) refers to *saṃskāra* (disposition) other than *bhāvanā* (mental impression); by this, *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) is also included.
In the root text, the term "general qualities" (*sāmānyaguṇāḥ*) is used; its true nature (*tattva*) consists in being distinct from color (*rūpa*) and touch (*sparśa*).

In this context, the delimitor of the property of being a substance-qualifier (dravyavibhājakatāvacchedaka) is "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, while its delimitor of pervasion (*tadvyāpyatāvacchedaka*) is "odorousness" (*gandhatva*) and so forth; [these are defined as] the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) that is devoid of any genus (*jāti*) residing in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), velocity (*vega*), or fluidity (*dravatva*), which serves as the delimitor of the pervasion of the qualifiers that differentiate substances.

The application of the definition [of substance] is established because that "otherness" (anya-tva) exists in number and the other categories. Here, in the case of the watery white color and the non-hot, non-cold touch of air,
there is a specific universal (jāti-viśeṣa) excluded from the white color and touch belonging to earth and the other substances.

The term "existent" (*sat*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to white color (*śuklarūpa*) and non-hot-non-cold touch (*anuṣṇāśītasparśa*), as there is no evidence for their being causes of destruction.
[This definition applies] to the disjunction between two hard parts delimited by a universal that delimits the status of being a generator of a specific sound;

to the excellence of velocity in fire; and to the fluidity residing in ghee and the like, which is delimited by a specific difference (*vaijātya*) that is the delimitant of the state of being destructible by absolute contact with fire.

The term "non-existence" (*avṛtti*) is a qualifier of the genus (*jāti*) in order to exclude non-pervasion; the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is for the purpose of excluding that [non-existence] from action (*karman*) and so forth. [This refers to] the absence of those respective numbers (*saṃkhyātva*) and so on, which serve as the delimiters of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) for earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and other such properties.
The term "jāti" (universal) is included to exclude under-extension (*avyāpti*) due to the absence [of such a universal] in number (*saṃkhyā*).

Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which delimits the delimiter of the differentiator of substance (*dravyavibhājakatāvacchedaka*) is intended here in terms of its specific individuality (*tattadvyaktitvena*), and not in terms of being such an adjunct; otherwise, even "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*) and so forth would [be included].

"Because it would result in the impossibility [of such a universal] due to being that kind of genus. In this root-text, regarding the statement "number and so forth up to remoteness, fluidity, and indeed viscidity," the word *sneha* (viscidity) is also indicative of *vega* (velocity). It will be stated later that elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Now, [an objection]: does not the property of being perceptible by two sense organs (*dvīndriyagrāhyatva*) over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to color and other qualities?
Because they can be apprehended even by the mind (*manas*), the definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) regarding the two types of sensory objects apprehended by the internal sense;

furthermore, since color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are apprehended by the pair of eyes and other senses, it would be under-extensive (*avyāpta*) regarding supersensuous (*atīndriya*) numbers and the like, as the property of being apprehended by a sense faculty (*indriyagrāhyatva*) is simply absent there. Therefore, he says: "by the eye and also by the skin."
The meaning of that [term] is the state of being perceivable by both the eye and the skin.

The precise definition (niṣkarṣa), however, is: the quality-ness (guṇatva) of that which inheres in a property other than a mental impression (bhāvanā) that is perceptible by both the eye and the skin. This is stated in order to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to mental impressions, which would otherwise occur if "the state of being a mental impression" (saṃskāratva) and so forth were included.

"Another [definition] is 'that which is the object of cultivation' (bhāvanāvṛtti). The inclusion of "quality-ness" (guṇatva) is for the purpose of excluding karma and so forth from that definition. Now, an objection:

the property of being "grasped by one or another external sense organ" is over-extensive (ativyāpta) with respect to number and the like, because even though those are grasped by both [the eye and the skin], their status as being grasped by one [of them] is not lost; furthermore, it is under-extensive (avyāpta) with respect to supersensible color-form and the like.
Since for those [entities] there is an absolute absence of being perceivable by the sense-faculties, he says: "of form and so forth" (*rūpādīnām*).

"By the eye and so forth" (*cakṣurādinā*) means "by the eye alone," and so on. Thus, because what is intended is the state of being perceivable by each individual faculty alone, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to number and the like, since they are not [perceived] in that way. This is because [they] are [only] perceivable [by multiple faculties].

Because they are capable of being apprehended, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) with respect to supersensuous forms and so forth. Thus, the intended meaning is that the definition of these [qualities] is:

"being a quality inherent in that which possesses motion, which is perceptible by an external sense organ, yet not perceptible by both the eye and the skin. Nor is there [non-pervasion] regarding the minimum magnitude (apakarṣa) residing in a triad (trasareṇu), since it is indeed perceived by the visual organ alone.
It should not be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case because the minimal degree of minuteness residing in a *trasareṇu* is perceived by the visual organ alone;
for a quality must also be qualified by its difference from other dimensions (*parimāṇa*). [End of] the root-text.
Regarding the phrase "the cultivation of gravity and the unseen force" (*gurutvādṛṣṭabhāvanā*), the term *bhāvanā* refers here to a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) distinct from velocity (*vega*);
by this, elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) is also included.
Furthermore, "transcendence of the senses" (*atīndriyatva*) does not mean being an object that is not a content of perception produced by the sense organs; for if that were the case...

It should not be argued that there is no possibility [of the definition applying] to gravity and so forth because they are objects of extra-sensory perception (*alaukika-pratyakṣa*), for the intended meaning is "not being an object of sensory perception" (*laukika-pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, it should not be said that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to supersensible form and so forth if this were the case.

Because what is intended is a quality-ness that inheres in a property other than *saṃskāratva* (the nature of being a latent impression) which occurs in a locus narrower than quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and resides in objects of worldly direct perception, the phrase "occurring in a locus narrower than quality-ness" is included to avoid the impossibility [of the definition] by taking *sat* (existence) and so forth.
The phrase "other than *saṃskāratva*" is included to avoid the non-pervasion [of the definition] regarding *bhāvanā* (mental impression) and *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity).

The term "quality" (guṇa) is included to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to genus (jāti) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "produced from qualities of a non-cause" (akāraṇaguṇotpanna) in the root text, the author of the Muktāvalī says "by the quality of the cause" (kāraṇaguṇena) in order to dispel the misconception that "non-cause" means "that which is not a cause" [and thus refers to something unrelated]. The meaning is: "by a quality inhering in the inherent cause" (samavāyikāraṇasamaveta-guṇena).

In this context, "causality" (kāraṇatva) is not intended; rather, it should be understood as mere "inherence" (samavāyitva). Regarding the phrase "not such as those," the analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: "produced by the qualities of the cause" means *kāraṇaguṇotpannāḥ*; "not produced by the qualities of the cause" means *akāraṇaguṇotpannāḥ*.

The meaning is as follows: [the definition of a quality] consists in being produced by a quality inherent in that which is inherent in its own substratum (svaśrayasamavāyisamaveta), being produced from the qualities of the cause (kāraṇaguṇotpanna), not being produced by such a quality (tādṛśaguṇājanyatva), and not having the qualities of a non-cause as its antecedent (akāraṇaguṇapūrvakatva).

Although this [definition] applies to eternal forms as well as to produced things such as those born of heating (pākaja), and to duality and separateness other than the duality and separateness belonging to parts and wholes;

Although [the definition] would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to conjunctions and disjunctions produced by action (*karmaja-saṃyoga-vibhāga*) and to fluidity produced by heating (*pākaja-dravatva*), which are pervaded by universals (*jāti*), there is no fault because what is intended is the state of possessing a universal that is directly subordinate to the genus of quality (*guṇatva*) and resides only in those qualities produced from non-causal qualities (*akāraṇaguṇotpanna-mātravṛtti*). And as for "residing only in those produced from non-causal qualities":
The state of being an obstruction produced by specific causal qualities;

the specific universal (vaijātya) residing in color that is delimited by being produced by maturation (pākaja); the specific universal residing in conjunction, disjunction, and velocity that is delimited by being produced by action; and the specific universal residing in atomic dimension (aṇu-parimāṇa).

The phrase "directly pervaded by the property of being a quality" (*guṇatvasākṣādvyāpya*) is included in order to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when taking "supreme greatness" (*paramamahattvatva*) as the subject. Its meaning is: being directly pervaded by the property of being a quality, while at the same time not being pervaded by any property other than the property of being a quality that is itself pervaded by the property of being a quality. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding mental impression (*bhāvanā*), because the property of being a mental impression (*bhāvanātva*) is not directly pervaded by the property of being a quality.
In this way as well, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition to *paratva* and *aparatva* remains;

however, that too should be understood as being refuted by qualifying the universal (*jāti*) with the condition of "not residing in *paratva* and *aparatva*. 90 || 91 || 92 || 93 || 94 || In the root [text], they arise from the qualities of their causes (*kāraṇaguṇodbhava*).
Thus, the previously mentioned definition of being produced by the qualities of its cause— namely,
"being produced by a quality inherent in that which is inherent in its own substratum"—

is also untenable, because it would over-extend (ativyāpti) to cases such as the conjunction and disjunction of the body with a book, which are produced by the conjunction and disjunction of the hand with the book.

Nor should it be argued that [the definition] is "being produced by a quality inherent in only those things in which its own substratum is inherent," because the conjunction between a hand and a book, for instance, is not inherent in only those things in which its own substratum is inherent;
for even so, there is oneness between the part and the whole.
Even so,
that [quality] consists in being produced by a quality of the same class (*sajātīya*) that inheres solely in what is inherent in its own substratum;
for there is no such sameness of class between the unity of a part and the duality of the whole-part.

That fault remains as it was, because what is intended is similarity (*sājātya*) by way of a genus that is pervaded by a genus which is itself pervaded by "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). Since there is indeed similarity between the parts and the whole, or between color and so forth, by way of "blueness" (*nīlatva*) and the like, there is no impossibility. [Objection: Even so, in the case of eternal form...
If it is argued that there is no pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of dimension produced by number and accumulation, or in the case of velocity produced by action, we say no;

for what is intended is the possession of a genus residing in that which is produced by a quality of the same class inhering in only those substances that are inherent in its own substratum. This applies to eternal color and so forth, by taking such [genuses] as "color-ness" and the like.

Because of the possession of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇasamanvayāt*). And here, that genus (*jāti*) should be qualified by being distinct from number-ness (*saṃkhyātva*) and separateness-ness (*pṛthaktvatva*), and by being other than the occurrence of the mental mode (*bhāvanāvṛtti*). Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to duality, dual separateness, and so forth, by taking such number-ness and separateness-ness as the basis.

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to mental impression (*bhāvanā*), by taking as the basis the quality-ness (*guṇatva*), the state of being a motion (*saṃskāratva*), and the existence residing in the motion of a whole produced by the motions of its nine parts. This is not so, because in a definition that incorporates a genus (*jāti*), what is intended is "not being produced by heat" (*apākajatva*) while possessing such a genus; thus, everything is consistent.
He states the purpose of the qualification "not produced by heating" (*apākaja*) in the delimiting condition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) in the *Muktāvalī*:
"of color and other qualities produced by heating" (*pākajarūpādīnām*).

This is because they lack the property of being preceded by the qualities of their causes, and thus the conventional usage of the term "preceded by the qualities of the cause" does not apply to them. Here...

It should be understood that for color, taste, smell, and touch produced by heating (*pākaja*), as well as fluidity produced by heating, duality and so forth, double separateness and so forth, conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority, there is neither the property of having qualities of the cause as their antecedent (*kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatva*) nor the property of not having qualities of the cause as their antecedent (*akāraṇaguṇapūrvakatva*). The same applies elsewhere. Now, regarding the root text beginning with "limited" (*prādeśika*):

The common property (*sādharmya*) of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, as well as the two types of pervasive particular qualities (*vibhu-viśeṣa-guṇa*), namely their non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*), must be demonstrated. In that regard, since the literal definition would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to action (*karman*) and the like, and under-extension (*avyāpti*) to the knowledge of God (*īśvara-jñāna*) and so forth, [the correct definition is]: "the state of possessing a universal (*jāti*) that is subsumed under the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and occurs in a non-pervasively occurring entity."

The meaning is "that which is to be awakened" (bodhyam). || 95 || 96 || In the root text, regarding the phrase "one-ness, separateness, moisture, and sound," one should understand that the meaning is "oneness and separateness. In the Vaiśeṣika [system], regarding the term "quality" (guṇa), it is to be construed with "of the self" (ātmanaḥ). In the Muktāvalī, regarding "hot touch," it refers to that which resides in the parts (avayava-gata).
The meaning is "hot touch"; that is, the hot touch residing in the composite whole.

Likewise, in what follows, this is intended to demonstrate that gravity is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) by means of both causal proximity to a single object (*kāraṇaikārthapratyāsatti*) and effectual proximity to a single object (*kāryaikārthapratyāsatti*).
Both [gravity and falling] have been mentioned in the phrase "of gravity and falling. The same applies further on.

In the *Saṃgraha*, regarding the specific conjunction of flour and so forth, the reading containing the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) in the nominative case—namely, "the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause"—is adopted, because there is a rule that an effect which is a positive entity must be produced by a non-inherent cause, and [this applies to] the conjunction of the drum and space.

The sense is that being an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) with respect to sound is necessary. Although the conjunction of the drum and the stick is an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for sound, it is not its *asamavāyikāraṇa*; rather, it is the conjunction of the drum and space (*ākāśa*) that is the *asamavāyikāraṇa*.

The point is this: although that [conjunction] does not possess a twofold causality as a single individual instance because it serves as a cause for that [effect] there, nevertheless, conjunction as a genus (*jāti*) certainly possesses a twofold causality. This applies similarly to the two types of conjunction and so forth mentioned later in the root text, following the word "tathā" (likewise) and preceding "dvidhaiva" (only in two ways).
Furthermore, the reading "parāparatva-dvitvādi-dvipṛthaktvādike" found in some manuscripts has entered [the text] through error, because since qualities such as remoteness (*paratva*) are not causes,
the two-fold causality [required for a universal] is absent therein. Nor indeed [is it the case that] remoteness and the like...
It should not be asked how [the absence] can be non-causal, since it is a cause with respect to the perception of its own destruction;
for it has been stated that it is a cause only with respect to perceptions other than the perception of destruction.
The details, however, should be sought elsewhere. [This concludes the section on] "non-pervasive occurrence" in the Muktāvalī.
By the words "the instructor" (*daiśika*) and so forth, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to [the case of] form (*rūpa*) and the rest. || 97 || 98 || 99 ||

By the phrase "blue-ness and so forth," red-ness and other such qualities are included. Otherwise, blue and the rest would constitute a single individual entity. Now, one might argue that the identity of individuals such as blue and red will be established simply on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*); to this, he says: "But parsimony... [is] "contradicted by perception. [For example: "The blue has perished."
The meaning is that [the claim] "red has arisen" and so forth is sublated by perception. As for the phrase "otherwise":
the meaning is the acceptance of the identity of blue, red, and so on, based merely on parsimony (*lāghava*).
[Objection: But is it not the case that from such cognitions as "the pot has arisen" and "the pot has perished,"...

To the objection that there is oneness in the case of a jar and so forth, he says: "by production," etc. By this—namely, by such a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates [the existence of] such a genus—[it is shown that] taste and so forth refers to tasteness and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), smellness and the like are included.

Anticipating the objection that the definition over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other categories, he says: "‘Perceptible by the eye’—this [means] of the phrase ‘perceptible by the eye’. Therefore, there is no tautology even though the term "eye" was previously taken as a *pratīka* (extracted citation). "Specific quality-ness" (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) means the state of being a distinct or unique quality.

And "distinctness" (vailakṣaṇya) consists in not being apprehended by anything other than the eye. Nor should it be argued that even so, there is over-extension (ativyāpti) to the conjunction of light and darkness;

for [the definition of] "being apprehended by the eye alone" would result in over-extension to specific types of moisture (sneha) apprehended by the eye alone, and thus [the definition of] "being apprehended by the eye alone" [must be qualified].

Since it is necessary to accept that the genus (*jāti*) is a qualifier and to intend the definition as "the quality possessing a genus perceivable by the eye alone," this very formulation excludes over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the conjunction between light and a jar; for [otherwise], one would have to take the genus of "lightness" (*prabhātva*) into account.
The term "quality" (guṇa) is included to exclude over-extension to light (prabhā). The same applies hereafter;
that is to say, this method should be understood to apply to the definitions of taste (rasa) and touch (sparśa) as well.
[The phrase] "lest there be the consequence of non-perceptibility" means [that it would otherwise follow] with respect to the visual perception of a substance (dravya-cākṣuṣa).
The sense is that [the cause] is the possession of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpatva*) by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Regarding the phrase "belonging to a genus that is pervasively present" (*vyāpyavṛttijātīya*): it should be understood that a genus residing in what is pervasively present is one that resides in that which has an object (*saviṣaya*).

Therefore, even though a cognition belonging to the same genus as the Lord's pervasively present cognition—such as our own cognition—is non-pervasively present (*avyāpyavṛtti*), [it does not follow that the definition fails].

There is no harm [to our position]. But one might object: even though there are many trees, just as one says "one forest," the experience of "one painting" can be accounted for by taking the singularity that belongs to the collection of forms; to this, he replies with the words "not so," because of the [unwarranted] complexity (gaurava) involved in [the view that] "painting" refers to...
The meaning is that it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate the status of being an object of cognition in multiple locations. Now, one might ask:

since in a jar or similar object which is the locus of a variegated color, the blue parts of the shards and other such causes exist through the relation of inherence in their own substratum (*svāśrayasamavetatva*), why is there no [cognition of variegation] there?

To the objection that there is no production of blue and so forth [from a variegated whole], he says: "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*). This means: and because the variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is established by the aforementioned parsimony (*lāghava*). "Due to the postulation of an obstructive relation" (*pratibandhakatvakalpanāt*): [this refers to] the state of being an obstructor of blue with respect to blue itself through the relation of "inherence in that which inheres in its own inherent substrate" (*svasamavāyisamavetatva*), and [the state of being an obstructor] of yellow color with respect to yellow color through the property of being a color other than blue (*nīlātiriktarūpatvena*).
By the principle that yellowness acts as an obstacle by virtue of being a color distinct from [other colors], one postulates a relationship of the obstructed and the obstructor; otherwise,
in the case of a jar produced from potsherds possessing various types of color, [there would be no obstruction] with respect to the delimitation of a blue potsherd and so forth.
The meaning is that the production of yellow is extremely difficult to prevent.

On this point, the moderns [Navīnas] argue: the aforementioned relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) is not required to prevent the occurrence of blue in a jar composed of potsherds possessing various types of color, by way of the delimitation of a yellow potsherd.

However, it is postulated that blue and so forth are causes of [the cognition of] blue and so forth by way of the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). But if a variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is accepted, then for the sake of blue and so forth by way of inherence,
there must be causality by way of the property of blueness (*nīlatva*) and so forth, through the relation of "inhering in what is inherent in its own substratum" (*svāśrayasamavetatva*).
They say that there is complexity (gaurava) because one must postulate the previously mentioned relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*).
That is not correct;

for even when one accepts the aforementioned causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) as being constituted by the relation of delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*), [the complexity remains] by virtue of the relation of delimitingness.

For you too, it is necessary that blue and so forth be a cause of blue and so forth by means of the relation of "being inherent in what is inherent in its own substratum," in order to prevent the production of blue and so forth in space and the like by way of inherence— just as [blue] is produced in a jar and the like when it arises in a potsherd and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the cognition "this is variegated," since it is simpler (lāghava) to postulate a single [variegated] entity than to postulate it in multiple locations,

the previously mentioned complexity of postulating a relationship between the sublated and the sublator does not constitute a fault once a distinct variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is established in accordance with this parsimony.
"Because it is from the perspective of the result," as explained at length elsewhere. Regarding the statement "touch (*sparśa*) has also been explained":

if one does not admit touch in a jar or similar object composed of parts possessing both soft and hard touches, it would follow that the jar is intangible; therefore, by such reasoning, a variegated touch (*citrasparśa*) is also necessarily required.

This is the state of affairs: even if the whole (*avayavin*) were devoid of rasa, there would be no harm [to the theory]. Nor should it be argued that a distinct "variegated" (*citra*) rasa is established because it is the object of the cognition "rasa is variegated. For such a cognition can be accounted for by the various rasas residing in the parts; otherwise, one would have to postulate a distinct variegated rasa, as well as its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), and so forth.

[This is] due to [the principle of] gravity (*gaurava*). Nor can it be argued that, because the taste of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is imperceptible and thus cannot serve as the determinant for the cognition of sweet and other tastes,
there must be a sweet and other tastes in the triad (*tryaṇuka*), and so on, up until the final composite substance (*antyāvayavin*), all of which possess sweet and other tastes.

It should not be argued that there is a lack of evidence [for the existence of taste], because the cognition of sweetness and so forth is established by the sweet taste residing in the triad (tryaṇuka) itself;

for, by the fact that the sweet taste in the triad would otherwise be inexplicable, the causal status of "sweetness" with respect to [the production of] a sweet taste [in a larger body] is established through the relation of inhering in that which inheres in its own substratum (svasamavāyisamavetatva).
Because such a cause has already been established, it would be impossible to avoid the production of sweet and other tastes in substances consisting of four atoms and the like.

100 || Now, one might object: "Let it be that baking occurs even in the parts of a jar, but not in the atoms. To this he says: "Not indeed [in the case of] red... and so on. The phrase "not residing in conjunction" (*na saṃyogagata*) means that the cognition "the conjunction is hard" actually apprehends the state of having a substance possessing a hard touch as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*). This is the intended meaning. ||101||102||103||104||

"The ripening (*pāka*) of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth" means the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of color-form and so forth. "Ripening is not possible" means that conjunction with fire (*tejaḥ-saṃyoga*) which has the transformation of color-form and so forth as its result is not possible; that is to say, the transformation of color-form is not possible.

Since the conjunction of fire is the cause for the destruction of color and other qualities— applying universally to both direct and indirect [destruction] by way of delimitation through all constituent parts— it is impossible for the destruction of color and other qualities to occur in the whole while its parts remain occupied by that [whole], because of that [conjunction].
The sense is that there is an absence of conjunction with light across all parts [of the object]. Nor should it be asked:
"Even when a jar or the like exists, why does conjunction with light not arise across all its parts? For it is thus...

At the time when the conjunction with fire is produced in the whole (avayavin) by way of delimitation through the conjunction that initiates [the process], there is a rule that either impulsion (nodana) or impact (abhighāta) must also be produced in the parts by way of that same delimitation; consequently, because an action caused by disjunction would arise in the parts, the initiating conjunction would be destroyed, which would entail the destruction of the whole.

Nor should it be argued that there is no obstacle to the acceptance of the destruction of color and other qualities in the whole prior to [the impact], since the destruction of the whole is possible at the very fifth moment immediately following the impact on the parts;
for in that case, the destruction of the previous whole and the production of another whole are both necessary.

Since there is no evidence for postulating a heterogeneous conjunction with fire that produces a transformation of color and other qualities in the prior whole, and because the destruction of the substratum is the cause for the destruction of the whole's color,
it would be cumbersome to include "not being produced by baking" within the definition of the effect; therefore, [the destruction of the whole occurs] without the destruction of the whole.

The underlying assumption is that since it is impossible for the form of the whole (avayavin) to be destroyed by baking, there would be the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the causality of the blue color of the parts toward the blue color of the whole; furthermore, it is impossible for blue and other qualities to be produced in the whole by baking once the whole has perished. [This refers to the phrase] "when the wholes have perished."

The sense is that, according to the previously stated method, destruction occurs—starting from the potsherds and other parts that initiate a jar, down to its constituent atoms, and extending up to the dyads (dvyaṇuka) of the jar and so forth—due to contact with fire. [This occurs] in independent [entities], which are characterized by the destruction of the effect-substance. Now, one might ask: why is there no difference in configuration (saṃsthāna-bheda) and so forth in those cases?
Because this is understood, he says: "of the luminaries. *Vyūha* means configuration (*saṃsthāna*). *Vaiśadya* means clarity (*utpati*).

*Prakriyā* refers to the description of the moment of origination and so forth, such as the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). The word "is performed" (*kriyate*) is to be supplied. [This refers to] the non-acceptance of disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*).

The meaning is that, just as there is a distinction between effect and non-effect based on the distinction between cause and non-cause, there is likewise a distinction of the mere cause based on the distinction between cause and non-cause; thus, the position is the non-acceptance of a distinction between cause and non-cause [arising] from a distinction between cause and non-cause.
